subject: Parameterizing OU and OUf's sigma and tau

messages.author: 96c6f8c408624a9c
messages.subject: Parameterizing OU and OUf's sigma and tau
parts:
Dear Christen,

I am trying to manually fit the OU and OUf models to my variogram and am having trouble understanding how to interpret the sigma and tau parameters in order to provide a range of values appropriate for my data. I have been testing out different values to see how it affects the fit to the variogram but I'm concerned that poorly fit values may impact the outcome of the weighted AKDE. It seems like sigma adjusts where the fitted line asymptotes - can you describe how tau changes the dynamics of the model fit? 

A secondary question is regarding the weighted AKDE. I have data that is duty cycled and would like to use the weighted option. Running the following AKDE : akde(one, M.OU, weights = TRUE) yesterday took ~ 2 hours. I am interested in testing out the various parameters in the bandwidth() argument to try to speed up the processing. Should the bandwidth() argument be run independently of the  akde() and saved as an object and then akde() references it automatically or does it need to be incorporated into the akde() argument?

Thank you so much for your time! I am very excited to apply your package to my deer movement data!

Best,
Meredith

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Parameterizing OU and OUf's sigma and tau
parts:
Hi Meredith,

The sigma parameter in the OU, OUf, and OUF models is indeed the asymptote of the variogram. The tau parameter in OU and OUf are different. In the OU model, there is a tau[position] parameter that is the timescale over which autocorrelation in location decays. This can be thought of as the home-range crossing timescale. In the OUF model, there is an additional tau[velocity] parameter that is the timescale over which autocorrelation in velocity decays. This can be thought of as the persistence of motion timescale. In the OUf model, the tau[position] and tau[velocity] parameters cannot be distinguished and only one parameter is estimated. So in this model, the animal is almost bee-lining back and forth across its home range. The ctmm.guess() function should be able to provide reasonable initial guesstimates for the parameters, as long as severe data quality isn't an issue. There should rarely be the need to do manual tinkering, especially as I have been improving ctmm's optimizer. Initial guesses usually only need to be in the ballpark for fitting.

I have some notes on what can slow down bandwidth/weight optimization with in help('bandwidth'). Those notes are updated in the development branch of ctmm on GitHub, which I have copied below. akde() calls bandwidth() when running and passes any arguments provided. You do not need to call bandwidth() directly in normal operation.

Best,
Chris

fast=TRUE grids the data with grid width dt and applies FFT algorithms, for a computational cost as low as O(n \log n) with only O(n) function evaluations. If no dt is specified, the minimum sampling interval min(diff(data$t)) is used. If the data are irregular (permitting gaps), then dt may need to be several times smaller to avoid slow down. In this case, try setting trace=TRUE and decreasing dt until the interations speed up and the number of feasibility assessments becomes less than O(n). On the other hand, if the data contain some very tiny time intervals, say 1 second among hourly sampled data, then the default dt setting will create an excessively high-resolution discretization of time, which will also cause slowdown. In this case CTMM should contain an error model and dt can likely be increased to a larger fraction of the median sampling interval.

fast=FALSE uses exact times and has a computational cost as low as O(n^2), including O(n^2) function evaluations. With PC="direct" this method will produce a result that is exact to within machine precision, but with a computational cost of O(n^3). fast=FALSE,PC='direct' is often the fastest method with small datasets, where n ≤ O(1,000), but scales terribly with larger datasets.

Yes, akde() passes those arguments to bandwidth(). The bandwidth() function is only exposed to users because I've had users with manuscript reviewers requesting the specific numbers on the bandwidth.

Best,
Chris
